title: Mali Gaura

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Nat Narain, and your line was slow the lively: once for the music, once for the words.

A postcard holds a few lines and a stamp. Nobody calls it a failed letter. Sometimes it's the thing that stays on the fridge for years, because it said one thing and said it well. Past Nat Narain in the Guru Granth Sahib, you come to a section with a postcard's size and its own full heading: Mali Gaura. It's short. It's complete. And it has a guest at the end.
screen: `A POSTCARD, NOT A FAILED LETTER.` → `A SHORT SECTION, ITS OWN HEADING.` → `MALI GAURA.`

segments.voice: First, Mali Gaura gets the same treatment as the long ragas: its own name at the top and an invocation of the One, Ik Onkar, Satgur Prasad, the One Creator, known by the Guru's grace. A short raga isn't an appendix. In the Granth, a few pages can be a whole room. Inside, the voices are Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and then, closing the section, Bhagat Namdev, a devotee whose hymns the Gurus gathered into the Granth beside their own. His verse is for tomorrow. Today, the opening. Guru Ram Das begins, in plain English, not word for word, with a picture of seekers: adepts, searchers and silent sages, all turning their minds toward the Lord with longing. It's a wide view for a small room. People known for hard practices are shown with the same longing anyone can have, and the hymn's answer is that the Guru shows them the unseen Lord. That's the sweetness of a short raga. No time to wander. It names the longing, points to the answer, and stops. Length isn't the measure here; a short shabad sung with attention is a complete offering. Mali Gaura says what it came to say, then hands the last word to a guest. That's today's line: short and sweet.
screen: `ITS OWN NAME, ITS OWN INVOCATION.` · `GURUS FIRST, NAMDEV LAST.` · `SEEKERS AND SAGES, ALL LONGING.` · `LENGTH ISN'T THE MEASURE.` · then, large: `SHORT AND SWEET.`

segments.voice: Choose one short word to stay with: if you pray, Waheguru; if you don't, simply the word here. Say it once, silently, and let it be complete, without stacking more words behind it. When the mind starts writing a longer letter, set the pen down and come back to the postcard: one word, one breath, each time enough on its own.
Mali Gaura. A short raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, with its own heading and invocation, where Gurus sing first and Bhagat Namdev closes. Today's word.
Your line: short and sweet. A few words, said with attention, can be a whole offering. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Each raga section of the Guru Granth Sahib is sung in its own raga in kirtan; shorter sections like Mali Gaura are drawn on just as the longer ones are, and a single shabad is a complete offering in a gurdwara program.
